title: U.S. Launches Sweeping H-1B and PERM Fraud Probe With Dozens of Subpoenas
excerpt: The Department of Labor's Inspector General has opened a major investigation into alleged visa fraud, wage theft, and human trafficking across H-1B and PERM labor certification programs, with IT firm Cognizant among companies under scrutiny.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The U.S. launched a major investigation into H-1B visa fraud on July 8, issuing numerous subpoenas.
  • Cognizant is under scrutiny due to whistleblower complaints, with other major employers also facing investigation.
  • H-1B visa approvals have sharply declined, with only 52,360 approved in fiscal year 2026 so far.
  • The investigation aims to combat worker exploitation and human trafficking linked to visa programs.
Scope of the Investigation
›Dozens of subpoenas issued by the Department of Labor.
›Coordinated with DOJ, DHS, and other federal agencies.
›Focus on false applications and wage-kickback schemes.
›Public reporting initiative for harmed workers launched.
  • The U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General launched a major fraud investigation into the H-1B visa and PERM labor certification programs on July 8, issuing dozens of subpoenas.
  • The probe is part of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, led by Vice President JD Vance, and involves the DOJ, DHS, and other federal agencies.
  • IT services firm Cognizant has been named by investigators based on whistleblower complaints, while other major H-1B-dependent employers face heightened scrutiny.
  • H-1B approvals have dropped sharply in fiscal year 2026, with just 52,360 new visas approved year-to-date compared with 113,485 in all of 2025.

The U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General has launched what it calls one of the most aggressive investigations ever into alleged fraud, worker exploitation, and human trafficking within the H-1B visa and PERM labor certification programs. The announcement, made on July 8, marks a major escalation in the Trump administration's enforcement posture toward employment-based immigration.

"My team, in conjunction with President Trump and Vice President Vance's Fraud Task Force, has worked relentlessly to uncover fraud, safeguard taxpayer dollars, and hold bad actors accountable," Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said in a statement. "For far too long, fraudsters believed they could game the U.S. employment-based visa system and get away with it. They were wrong."

The Scope of the Investigation

The probe is being coordinated across multiple federal agencies, including the Department of Justice, Department of Homeland Security, and others operating under the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, established by executive order in March and led by Vice President JD Vance. Investigators have already issued dozens of subpoenas and are preparing affidavits for search warrants, according to D'Esposito.

The investigation is examining allegations that some employers and labor brokers submitted false applications, arranged coercive wage-kickback schemes, paid workers below required wages, placed sponsored employees at unlisted worksites, or exploited foreign workers through trafficking-like conditions. The government has also launched a public reporting initiative for workers who believe they have been harmed by H-1B or PERM-related misconduct.

"D'Esposito told Fox News that the government has "received intel from whistleblowers" about the company."

"This isn't just paperwork fraud — it's the exploitation of vulnerable workers, forced labor, the displacement of American workers, and abusive human trafficking."

— Anthony D'Esposito, Inspector General, U.S. Department of Labor

Cognizant Named; Broader Industry Under Watch

IT services firm Cognizant, which has the majority of its workforce in India and is one of the largest users of H-1B visas, has been specifically named based on whistleblower complaints. D'Esposito told Fox News that the government has "received intel from whistleblowers" about the company. Cognizant has not publicly responded to the allegations, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

The company also faces a separate False Claims Act lawsuit in the Third Circuit, brought by whistleblower Jean-Claude Franchitti, alleging that Cognizant improperly applied for cheaper L-1 and B-1 visas instead of H-1B visas and underpaid workers, according to Bloomberg Law.

Other top H-1B users — including Amazon, Infosys, TCS, IBM, and Microsoft — have not been individually named in the investigation, but the probe's sweeping scope has put the entire ecosystem on alert. Microsoft drew particular scrutiny this month after its Xbox gaming division laid off 1,600 workers despite the parent company being approved for 2,273 H-1B visas this fiscal year.

The investigation arrives amid a steep decline in H-1B visa approvals. According to data from HR services firm Xpheno, just 52,360 new H-1B visas have been approved in fiscal year 2026 year-to-date, compared with 113,485 in all of 2025 and 139,692 in 2024. There are currently about 730,000 H-1B visa holders in the United States, with Indian nationals receiving approximately 70 percent of all approved petitions.

A previous effort to impose a $100,000 supplemental fee on new H-1B petitions was struck down by a federal judge in June, and in May, the administration's fraud task force identified more than 10,000 cases of foreign students in the Optional Practical Training program claiming employment with suspect or nonexistent employers.

What Employers and Workers Should Know

Immigration attorneys say the investigation does not end the H-1B or PERM programs, nor does it automatically revoke approved petitions. But employers should expect increased scrutiny and longer processing times. Wilner & O'Reilly, an immigration law firm, advises employers to conduct compliance reviews confirming that Labor Condition Applications are accurate, public access files are complete, sponsored employees are being paid correctly, and any worksite or duty changes have been documented.

For PERM cases, employers should preserve recruitment materials, applicant resumes, interview notes, and records showing that positions represent genuine job opportunities. "Records should be complete and truthful; they should never be recreated or altered to conceal a past problem," the firm warned.

H-1B workers, meanwhile, should retain copies of approval notices, pay statements, tax documents, and employment agreements, and should understand what was filed on their behalf. Workers concerned about employer fraud may be able to transfer to a new employer through H-1B portability, but should seek legal advice before making any changes.

What Comes Next

The investigation is expected to produce criminal referrals, and Congress is simultaneously considering broader changes to the H-1B program, with some Republican lawmakers pushing for its abolition. Rep. Riley Moore of West Virginia told Fox News that the program is "a scam" that has been "perpetrated on the American worker for far too long."

For Indian IT firms and the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals working in the United States on H-1B visas, the coming months are likely to bring heightened compliance demands, more frequent audits, and greater uncertainty in an already difficult immigration environment.
